title: Cycle of poverty

definition.text: A situation, also called a poverty trap, in which poverty seems to be passed down, so that later generations cannot escape it.

facts.text: Self-reinforcing mechanisms keep poverty going once it exists, unless someone from outside steps in.
Applied to developing countries, the same idea is called a development trap.
Lack of money, education and social connections all help keep poor families in the cycle.
Children are the most vulnerable, since they depend on guardians and are too young to work their own way out.
The cycle of poverty makes the harms of climate change worse.
People living in degraded ecosystems and a poverty trap may want sustainable options but cannot afford to let ecosystems and resources regenerate.
Conditional cash transfers aim to help poor families now and to break the cycle for the next generation by building their skills and health.

notes: Much of the page is about US social policy (minimum wage, schooling, incarceration); not used.

definition.text: The ways whole poor countries stay stuck in poverty, through causes such as lack of credit, environmental degradation, corruption, disease, war and poor infrastructure.

facts.text: Extreme environmental degradation is one cause, because it reduces how much farmland can produce.
Jeffrey Sachs argues the extreme poor lack six kinds of capital, including natural capital, and capital per person can fall each generation when population grows faster than savings.
Sachs argues that large, lasting foreign aid can raise the capital stock enough to lift households above subsistence.
He wants public money to go to health, education, infrastructure and natural capital such as conserving biodiversity and ecosystems, leaving business investment to private firms.

definition.text: An idea from development and environmental studies about how people, especially vulnerable groups, can support themselves in ways that last and can recover from shocks.

facts.text: It widens poverty studies beyond material want to include vulnerability and social exclusion.
The idea was introduced by the Brundtland Commission, and the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development made sustainable livelihoods a broad goal for ending poverty.
The approach seeks human-centered, participatory development that links concern for environmental and economic resources.
The UN Sustainable Development Goals, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals for 2030, are an example; the COVID-19 pandemic set back goals such as SDG 1, No Poverty.

title: Livelihood capitals framework

definition.text: The United Nations Development Programme's way of assessing livelihoods by the five kinds of capital people can draw on: human, social, natural, physical and financial.

facts.text: How much access people have to these assets shapes how the UNDP designs its development projects.
The approach also looks at how people use their assets to cope with shocks and stresses.
The UK's Department for International Development and CARE also use sustainable livelihood frameworks in place of sector-by-sector approaches.

notes: Requires 'Natural capital' from elsewhere in the course.
